## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Nakulajātaka* (Ja 165) is a short birth story preserved in the Pali *Jātaka* collection. In the commentary edited by V. Fausböll, the verse opens with the line *Sandhiṁ katvā amittena* [Fausböll 1879]. The frame narrative takes place while the Buddha is residing at Jetavana and is delivered concerning two quarreling royal officers or ministers (*dve mahāmattā*) [Fausböll 1879]. As indicated by both the commentary and the canonical framing, the circumstances of the introductory episode match those of the earlier *Uragajātaka* [Fausböll 1879].

To demonstrate that he had reconciled these two individuals in a previous existence as well, the Buddha recounts an *atītavatthu* (story of the past) in which he was an ascetic who established peace between an innate pair of enemies: a snake (*sappa*) and a mongoose (*nakula*) [Fausböll 1879]. After admonishing them not to harbor suspicion or breach their concord, the ascetic cultivated the four divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*) and was destined for the Brahma realm [Fausböll 1879]. In the *samodhāna* (recapitulation of characters), the Buddha identifies the snake and the mongoose as the two ministers in their present lives, while he himself was the peacemaking hermit [Fausböll 1879].
